summary: This program brews coffee through a helper method that validates its arguments, and when the arguments are wrong it throws a custom exception class written specifically for this program. The first call succeeds and prints a brewing message; the second call asks for zero shots, so the program stops with a CoffeeConjuringException.

lines.text: A valid order: the method runs all the way through and prints the brewing messages.
Zero shots is invalid, so this call throws the custom exception and ends the program before main finishes.

lines.code: static void makeCoffee(String type, int shots) {
lines.text: The helper method takes the drink name and the shot count as parameters; being static means main can call it without creating an object.
Guard clauses at the top of a method reject bad input before any real work happens. Checking for null first matters, because calling isBlank on a null reference would itself crash.

lines.code: throw new CoffeeConjuringException("Coffee type must not be null or blank.");
lines.text: The throw statement immediately abandons the method and hands the exception object to the caller, carrying a message that explains what went wrong.

lines.code: throw new CoffeeConjuringException("Shots must be at least 1. Provided: " + shots);
lines.text: Including the offending value in the message makes the failure far easier to diagnose than a bare "invalid input".
A local variable holding an intermediate calculation; it exists only while this method is running.
The comparison produces true or false, which is stored in a boolean so the condition reads clearly below.
Naming the condition means the if statement reads like English instead of repeating the arithmetic.
A custom exception is just a class that extends an existing exception type. Extending RuntimeException makes it unchecked, so callers are not forced to catch it or declare it.
The constructor passes the message up to RuntimeException, which stores it so it appears in the stack trace.

lines.code: CoffeeConjuringException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
lines.text: A second constructor lets you attach the original exception as the cause when you wrap a lower-level failure, preserving the full chain of what went wrong.
